title: System Design Foundations
description: Measurement, scaling, caching, queues, and failure handling, with a short lesson for each topic.

cards.question: What is throughput?
cards.answer: Throughput is the amount of work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second or messages per second.

cards.question: What is scalability?
cards.answer: Scalability is a system's ability to handle more load by adding resources, without an unacceptable loss of latency, throughput, or reliability.

cards.question: What is latency?
cards.answer: Latency is the time one operation takes to complete, measured from the caller's point of view.

cards.question: Why are percentile latencies more useful than averages?
cards.answer: Percentiles show how slow the tail of requests is. An average can hide a small but important group of very slow requests.

cards.question: What does a p99 latency of 800 milliseconds mean?
cards.answer: Ninety-nine percent of requests finish in 800 milliseconds or less, and the slowest one percent take longer.

cards.question: What is availability?
cards.answer: Availability is the fraction of time or requests for which a service can successfully do its intended job.

cards.question: How is reliability different from availability?
cards.answer: Availability means the service answers. Reliability means it keeps producing correct results over time, even during expected failures.

cards.question: What is durability?
cards.answer: Durability is the promise that data, once acknowledged, stays stored despite failures within the system's stated fault model.

cards.question: What is an error budget?
cards.answer: An error budget is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows. Teams spend it on changes, and slow down releases when it runs low.

cards.question: What is capacity planning?
cards.answer: Capacity planning estimates future resource needs from expected load, growth, and safety margins, so the system meets its targets before it saturates.

cards.question: What is vertical scaling?
cards.answer: Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, memory, or storage. It is simple, but it hits hardware limits and keeps one large failure domain.

cards.question: What is horizontal scaling?
cards.answer: Horizontal scaling adds more machines or service instances and spreads the work across them, which requires distribution and coordination.

cards.question: What is a failure domain?
cards.answer: A failure domain is the set of components that fail together. One large machine is one large failure domain.

cards.question: Why is stateless application logic easier to scale horizontally?
cards.answer: Any instance can handle any request because durable state lives elsewhere, so instances can be added, removed, or replaced freely.

cards.question: What does a load balancer do?
cards.answer: A load balancer distributes requests across backend instances and removes unhealthy instances from rotation.

cards.question: What problem do health checks solve?
cards.answer: Health checks let routing avoid instances that cannot safely serve traffic, so fewer requests reach failed or unready nodes.

cards.question: What is round-robin load balancing?
cards.answer: Round robin sends each new request to the next backend in turn. It is simple but ignores differences in request cost and backend load.

cards.question: When is least-connections load balancing useful?
cards.answer: It helps when requests are long-lived or uneven, because it favors backends with fewer active connections.

cards.question: What is the trade-off of sticky sessions?
cards.answer: Sticky sessions let in-memory session state work, but they weaken load balancing and make failover harder.

cards.question: Why can CPU-only autoscaling fail?
cards.answer: A service may run out of memory, connections, queue capacity, or downstream quota long before its CPU becomes busy.

cards.question: What is a cache?
cards.answer: A cache is temporary storage for expensive or frequently used data, so later reads can skip recomputing or refetching it.

cards.question: What is cache hit rate?
cards.answer: Hit rate is the fraction of reads served from the cache instead of the underlying source. A higher rate means more backend work is avoided.

cards.question: How does cache-aside work?
cards.answer: The application checks the cache first, reads the source on a miss, and then stores the result in the cache.

cards.question: What is write-through caching?
cards.answer: Writes pass through the cache, which updates the backing store before confirming. Cache and source stay in step, but writes are slower.

cards.question: What is the risk of write-back caching?
cards.answer: Writes are confirmed before they reach the backing store, so data can be lost if the cache fails before flushing.

cards.question: What is cache invalidation?
cards.answer: Cache invalidation removes or expires cached data when it may no longer match the source of truth.

cards.question: Why is cache invalidation difficult?
cards.answer: Copies can outlive updates, invalidation messages can be delayed or lost, and one change can affect many cached results.

cards.question: What is a cache stampede?
cards.answer: Many requests miss the same hot key at once and all hit the backend together, which can overwhelm it.

cards.question: Why add jitter to cache expiration times?
cards.answer: Randomized expirations stop many keys from expiring at the same moment and causing a synchronized surge of backend traffic.

cards.question: What is a CDN?
cards.answer: A content delivery network serves cached content from locations close to users, which cuts network distance and origin load.

cards.question: What is a queue used for in system design?
cards.answer: A queue stores work until consumers can process it, which decouples producers from consumers and smooths out bursts.

cards.question: What trade-off does asynchronous messaging introduce?
cards.answer: It improves decoupling and burst handling, but results arrive later and the system must handle retries, duplicates, ordering, and visibility.

cards.question: What is at-most-once delivery?
cards.answer: A message is delivered zero or one time. There are no duplicates, but work can be lost if a failure happens before processing.

cards.question: What is at-least-once delivery?
cards.answer: The system retries until delivery seems successful, so work is not intentionally lost, but consumers can receive duplicates.

cards.question: Why is exactly-once delivery difficult?
cards.answer: After a failure, it can be unclear whether work finished before the acknowledgment was lost. Systems usually make the effect exactly-once instead.

cards.question: What is an idempotent operation?
cards.answer: An operation is idempotent when repeating it with the same request produces the same final result as doing it once.

cards.question: How does an idempotency key help an API?
cards.answer: The client sends a stable request identifier, and the server stores the outcome, so a retry returns the original result instead of repeating the change.

cards.question: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.answer: A dead-letter queue holds messages that keep failing, so they stop blocking normal traffic and can be inspected and replayed later.

cards.question: What is backpressure?
cards.answer: Backpressure makes producers slow down, wait, or get rejected when consumers cannot keep up, which prevents unbounded queues.

cards.question: What is load shedding?
cards.answer: Load shedding deliberately rejects low-priority or excess work when capacity runs out, so the system keeps serving what matters most.

cards.question: What is a single point of failure?
cards.answer: It is one component whose failure can make the whole service unavailable. Redundancy and failover are the usual ways to remove it.

cards.question: What is redundancy?
cards.answer: Redundancy keeps several components able to do the same critical job, so one failure does not stop the service.

cards.question: What is failover?
cards.answer: Failover switches traffic or responsibility from a failed component to a healthy replacement, either automatically or manually.

cards.question: What is fault tolerance?
cards.answer: Fault tolerance is the ability to keep providing acceptable service while some components have failed.

cards.question: Why are timeouts necessary in distributed calls?
cards.answer: Without a timeout, a caller can wait forever on a failed dependency. A timeout frees resources and lets recovery logic run.

cards.question: Why can retries make an outage worse?
cards.answer: Many clients retrying a struggling dependency multiply its load exactly when capacity is lowest, causing a retry storm.

cards.question: What is exponential backoff?
cards.answer: Each retry waits longer than the previous one, giving a struggling dependency time to recover.

cards.question: Why add jitter to retry backoff?
cards.answer: Randomness stops many clients from retrying at the same moments and creating repeated traffic spikes.

cards.question: What does a circuit breaker do?
cards.answer: After repeated failures it stops normal calls to a dependency for a while and fails fast, then sends a few probes to test recovery.

cards.question: What is graceful degradation?
cards.answer: Graceful degradation keeps core features working while turning off nonessential ones during failures or overload.
